headline: I spent three days convincing the election office I am actually a sentient collection of breakfast habits
body:
When I saw the draft rolls for the Graduates' constituency were out, I assumed my name would be listed as a simple taxpayer. Instead, the official told me my voter profile had been flagged because my primary qualification was listed as 'Expertise in identifying high-quality fermented batter' rather than an academic degree. I spent the next 72 hours in a windowless office trying to explain that, in this city, a three-decade commitment to finding the perfect masala dosa is practically a Doctorate in Applied Gastronomy.

The clerk, a man who seemed to view my life's work with profound skepticism, kept asking me for a 'Transcript of Credentials.' I offered him my punch card from the local tiffin centre, which showed I had successfully navigated 1,400 consecutive morning rushes without losing my temper or my spoon. Apparently, the Election Commission doesn't consider 'Ability to secure the last remaining table at 8:30 AM' a valid professional certification for the Legislative Council.

I eventually had to submit an affidavit signed by three neighborhood aunties who could attest to my sophisticated palate for filter coffee. They looked at my application, stamped it 'Non-Academic but Socially Integral,' and told me I was officially on the rolls. I’m not sure what the Legislative Council plans to do about the rising price of lentils, but I feel like I finally have the parliamentary credentials to make a stand.

igHook: Would you try to register your breakfast habits as a professional qualification?

judgeVerdict.reasoning: Candidate 7 takes a relatable, mundane cultural obsession (the masala dosa/filter coffee culture) and treats it with the grave, absurd weight of academic accreditation. It avoids the tired 'government-is-an-AI-glitch' trope found in almost every other candidate, offering a specific, character-driven narrative that feels both fresh and warm.

safetyVerdict.reasoning: The article is a harmless satirical piece about bureaucracy and personal food habits. It does not name any real individuals, public figures, or protected groups, and the image prompt is generic.
